sections.h2: Where is Washington, Utah, and how large is it?
sections.html:
Washington is a city in Washington County in the southwest corner of Utah, and it is part of the St. George metropolitan area. It sits at about 2,894 feet in elevation, a few miles east of St. George along Interstate 15.

The city is the second largest in the county. The 2020 census counted 27,993 people, up from 18,761 in 2010 and 8,186 in 2000. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate, shown at the top of this page, is 37,107.

Wikipedia lists the neighborhoods as old town Washington, Buena Vista, Green Springs and the Washington Fields area in the north. Older streets near the original townsite look quite different from the planned subdivisions that went up after 2000, so a seller on one side of town can face a very different buyer pool than a seller on the other.

sections.h2: What is the history of Washington City?
sections.html:
Washington was settled in 1857, when the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints sent 28 families to grow cotton in the desert. The mission was led by Robert Dockery Covington, a former Mississippi plantation owner, and a cotton mill operated in the town.

The name honors George Washington. The region picked up the nickname "Utah's Dixie" from the cotton-growing southeastern states, and the city has been using the shorter name "Washington City" in recent years. The old Washington School building now houses the city's historical museum.

For most of the twentieth century the town stayed small. Its population was 435 in 1950 and only 750 in 1970. Growth started in the 1980s and then sped up, which explains why so many houses in the city are less than twenty-five years old.

sections.h2: How does the desert climate affect a Washington house?
sections.html:
Washington has a hot, dry desert climate, and the roof, cooling system and exterior finishes take most of the wear. Official climate figures for neighboring St. George, which shares the same valley, show an average July high of 101.9 degrees and an average January low of 28.4 degrees.

St. George sees about 60 afternoons a year above 100 degrees and roughly 9 inches of precipitation, with only about an inch of snow. The record high there is 118 degrees, set on July 4, 2007.

Buyers walking through a Washington house tend to look hard at a few things:

  • The age and efficiency of the air conditioner, since it runs for months.
  • Roof underlayment and tile or shingle condition after years of sun.
  • Stucco cracks, faded paint and sun damage on south-facing walls and decks.
  • Irrigation lines and pool equipment, which fail more often in extreme heat.

Deferred work on any of these is a common reason a listed house sits. It is also a common reason owners look at an as-is sale, where the buyer takes the condition as it stands.

sections.h2: How do water rules affect landscaping and resale in Washington?
sections.html:
Water is the main long-term constraint in Washington County, and it shapes what a yard can look like. The Washington County Water Conservancy District reports that the county's population centers depend on the Virgin River basin and use more than 90% of the reliable annual supply.

In response, most cities in the county adopted rules that cap grass on new residential lots at 8% of the lot, with a separate cap for large lots. Grass is banned in park strips, in areas narrower than 8 feet and on slopes. Developers must use secondary or reuse water for irrigation where it is available, and potable water irrigation is banned from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. during summer months. The district also approved an excessive water use fee of $1.00 per 1,000 gallons for users above a set monthly volume.

The district's materials do not say how each rule applies in Washington City, so check the city's landscape and water conservation form before you change a yard. For a seller the practical point is simple: a large lawn on an older lot costs more to keep up, and buyers know it.

sections.h2: What roads, schools and shopping areas matter to buyers?
sections.html:
Washington is in the Washington County School District, and the city has its own set of nearby schools. Elementary schools inside city limits are Coral Canyon, Horizon, Majestic Fields, Riverside and Washington. Secondary schools in the city include Washington Fields Intermediate, Crimson Cliffs Middle and Crimson Cliffs High. Northern parts of the city feed into Fossil Ridge Intermediate, Pine View Middle and Pine View High in St. George.

A 2022 retail profile prepared for the city says Washington has three exits off Interstate 15 and calls Exit 13 the gateway to Washington County. It lists a Walmart Supercenter, The Home Depot, Kohl's, Best Buy, Albertsons and In-N-Out near Exit 10, and describes a hospital, an auto mall and the Green Springs master-planned community at Exit 13.

The same profile reports that the city added more than 3,300 homes between 2017 and 2021, including higher-density multifamily buildings near Exit 13. That much new supply competes with resale houses, which matters when you set an asking price. The profile counted 30,849 residents in 2022 and a median household income of $68,264.

sections.h2: What permits and city rules matter before selling a Washington house?
sections.html:
Any work you finish before listing should have a permit, and Washington City's Building Department issues them. The department handles single-family permits, additions, basement finishes, demolition, detached accessory buildings, garages and shops, sheds and patio covers, swimming pools and solar.

  • Applications and inspection requests run through the City Inspect portal. Requests in by 5 p.m. on a business day are typically handled the next business day.
  • Construction hours are 6 a.m. to 10 p.m., and concrete may start at 3 a.m. from April through October.
  • Accessory dwelling units may need a deed restriction.
  • The Building Department is at 111 North 100 East and can be reached at (435) 656-6326.

Unpermitted work, such as a finished basement, tends to surface when a buyer's inspector looks closely. Talk to the department before you list if you are unsure what was done to the house.

sections.h2: How do property tax and recording work when a Washington house sells?
sections.html:
Real property taxes in Washington County are due November 30 each year, and the lien follows the property, not the owner. The County Treasurer mails a notice to each owner, and title companies prorate the taxes at closing. Partial payments of $10 or more per parcel are accepted at any time, but the Treasurer's Office does not offer payment plans on delinquent taxes. Properties delinquent for at least five years can go to the county's tax sale held each May.

A primary residence in Utah is assessed on 55% of its market value because of a 45% residential exemption. A second home or an unoccupied house is taxed at the full value, which is worth checking if you own a house you no longer live in.

Deeds are recorded with the Washington County Recorder at 111 East Tabernacle Street in St. George. The posted fee is $45.00 per document plus $2.00 for each legal description over ten. The recorder does not accept recordings after 4:45 p.m. Mountain Time.

sections.h2: What are the ways to sell a house in Washington, UT?
sections.html:
You can list with an agent, sell it yourself, or accept a cash offer from an investor, and each route trades speed against price and effort. A listing usually brings the widest pool of buyers but also showings, inspection requests and a closing date that depends on the buyer's loan.

A cash sale fits best when the house needs work, when you are relocating, or when you inherited a property in Washington County and do not want to manage it. Cash Home Buyers works with owners of houses in any condition, and you can ask for an offer without committing to it.

sections.h2: What problems do Washington sellers usually run into?
sections.html:
Most sellers in Washington face a short list of practical problems, and knowing them early saves time.

  • Heat damage to roofs, stucco and cooling equipment that a buyer will price in.
  • Heirs who inherit a house in Washington County and live in another state.
  • Owners of second homes who find the property taxed at the full rate.
  • Competition from the large number of new houses built near Exit 13 and in the Washington Fields area.
  • Unfinished or unpermitted work discovered during a buyer's inspection.

If one of these fits, start by gathering the deed, the latest tax notice and any permit records.

faqs.q: Is Washington, UT the same as Washington County?
faqs.a: No. Washington is a city, and Washington County is the county that contains it along with St. George, Hurricane and other communities. Property tax bills and deeds in the city go through county offices in St. George.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Washington, Utah?
faqs.a: Real property taxes are due November 30 each year. The Washington County Treasurer mails the notice, and if you never receive one you are still responsible for the bill. The Treasurer's Office can send a copy on request.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Washington County?
faqs.a: The Recorder's posted fee is $45.00 per document, plus $2.00 for each legal description over ten. Recordings are not accepted after 4:45 p.m. Mountain Time.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for work on my Washington house?
faqs.a: Usually yes for additions, basement finishes, pools, solar and detached buildings. Washington City's Building Department issues permits through its City Inspect portal. Call (435) 656-6326 if you are not sure.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Washington house that needs repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. Houses are sold in any condition, and an as-is sale to a cash buyer is one way to avoid paying for repairs first.
